chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading a Deal as an Investor

lessons.title: Case Study: The HDFC Ltd and HDFC Bank Merger

children.text: On 4 April 2022, India's largest housing finance company announced it would merge into India's largest private sector bank, the very bank it had helped set up in 1994. Valued at roughly $40 billion, it was the biggest deal in Indian corporate history. You have already met pieces of it in this course: the 42 for 25 swap ratio, the fifteen-month approval path, the cancelled cross-holding. This lesson puts the pieces together and runs the deal through every tool from Chapters 1 to 3, the way you would for any merger in your own portfolio.

body.text: The HDFC merger was driven more by regulation and funding than by growth. Converting shares on the record date was the easy part for investors. What actually shaped returns afterwards was how quickly the combined bank could fund a large loan book with deposits.

children.text: Step 1: Classify the Deal

body.caption: The HDFC merger through Chapter 1 and 2 lenses

cells: Merger, acquisition or demerger?
Merger (amalgamation) under a scheme of arrangement
Which company survived?
HDFC Bank. HDFC Ltd was dissolved and delisted
Deal type
A reverse merger in the parent into subsidiary sense: HDFC Ltd owned about 21% of HDFC Bank and merged into it
Consideration
Shares only: 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares, or 1.68 per share
Cross-holding
HDFC Ltd's shares in HDFC Bank were cancelled on the merger
Key approvals
BSE, NSE and SEBI, RBI, CCI, other sector regulators, shareholders and creditors, NCLT Mumbai
Effective date and record date
1 July 2023 and 13 July 2023

children.text: Step 2: Understand Why It Happened
In October 2021, the RBI announced its
scale-based regulation

framework for NBFCs, which brought the largest non-bank lenders, including housing finance companies like HDFC Ltd, closer to bank-style rules. The gap between running a giant housing finance company and running a bank was narrowing. At the same time, the two companies had complementary strengths.

markDefs.definition: The RBI's layered regulatory framework for NBFCs, effective from October 2022, under which larger and more systemically important NBFCs face progressively stricter capital, governance and exposure rules.

columns.label: HDFC Ltd
points: India's leading home loan franchise with long customer relationships
Funded largely through bonds, bank borrowings and term deposits
No access to low-cost current and savings account deposits
Controlling stakes in HDFC Life, HDFC ERGO and HDFC AMC

columns.label: HDFC Bank
points: Large branch network and a deposit franchise including low-cost CASA
Millions of retail customers, few of whom held an HDFC home loan
Strong in unsecured retail, corporate and SME lending
Could offer home loans to its customers directly after the merger

children.text: Map that onto the motives from Lesson 1.2 and you get three of them at once:
funding cost synergy
(cheaper deposits replacing costlier borrowings over time),
revenue synergy
(cross-selling home loans to bank customers and bank products to home loan customers), and
simplification
(removing a listed holding company layer and a large cross-holding).

body.text: Notice which synergies were the most dependable. The simplification was certain on completion. The funding benefit depended on how fast the bank could raise deposits. The cross-selling was the least certain of all. As Lesson 1.2 warned, revenue synergies deserve the most scepticism, however strong the brand.

children.text: Step 3: Work Out What Happened to Your Shares

body.title: An odd-lot holding
body.prompt: Anjali held 110 HDFC Ltd shares on the record date. At 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares, how many whole HDFC Bank shares were credited to her demat account?
body.explanation: 110 × 42 ÷ 25 = 4,620 ÷ 25 = 184.8. She receives 184 whole shares. Under the usual scheme treatment described in Lesson 1.1, her 0.8 fractional entitlement is pooled with other fractions, sold, and paid to her in cash.

children.text: Now the ownership split. The figures below are rounded approximations, good enough to see how the 41% outcome arises.

stats.label: Held by HDFC Ltd and cancelled
HDFC Ltd shares outstanding
stats.context: Each converts into 1.68 HDFC Bank shares

body.caption: The cancelled cross-holding shrinks the existing base before the new shares are added.

body.title: What if the cross-holding had not been cancelled?
body.prompt: Using the same rounded figures, suppose HDFC Ltd's 117 crore HDFC Bank shares had somehow stayed outstanding. What percentage of HDFC Bank would former HDFC Ltd shareholders have owned through the new shares alone? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 311 ÷ (558 + 311) = 311 ÷ 869 = 35.8%. The difference from 41% shows why cross-holdings matter. HDFC Ltd's shareholders already owned that 21% stake indirectly. Cancelling it simply let them hold their share of HDFC Bank directly instead of through a holding company.

body.title: HDFC Bank ownership after the merger (approximate)
What did you really own after 4 April 2022?
body.question: You held HDFC Ltd shares on the announcement day and kept them until the record date in July 2023. Once the swap ratio was fixed, what mainly drove the value of your holding over those fifteen months?
options: HDFC Ltd's own home loan growth each quarter
HDFC Bank's share price, multiplied by 1.68, adjusted for a small arbitrage spread
The swap ratio, which changed each quarter to reflect results
Nothing, because shares under a pending merger are frozen
body.explanation: As Lesson 2.2 showed, a fixed swap ratio ties the target's value to the acquirer's price. HDFC Ltd traded broadly in line with 1.68 times HDFC Bank's price, less a spread for time and deal risk from Lesson 3.2. HDFC Ltd shareholders were effectively HDFC Bank shareholders from announcement day.

children.text: Step 4: Watch the Integration

The combined bank inherited HDFC Ltd's large loan book, but not a matching pool of deposits, because housing finance companies fund themselves mainly through borrowings. Overnight, the bank's loans grew much faster than its deposits. The metric investors watched was the
credit-deposit ratio
, which went above 100% after the merger.

markDefs.definition: Also called the loan-to-deposit ratio. A bank's advances divided by its deposits. Above 100% means the bank lends more than it holds in deposits and must fund the gap with borrowings, which are usually costlier.

body.caption: A bank that lends more than it takes in as deposits has to borrow the difference.

body.title: Why the ratio jumped
body.prompt: Use simplified, illustrative figures. A bank has advances of ₹16 lakh crore and deposits of ₹19 lakh crore. It merges with a housing finance company that has advances of ₹6 lakh crore and deposits of just ₹1 lakh crore. What is the combined credit-deposit ratio, in percent?
body.explanation: Before the merger, the bank's ratio was ₹16 lakh crore ÷ ₹19 lakh crore = 84%. Combined advances = ₹22 lakh crore and combined deposits = ₹20 lakh crore, so the ratio is 22 ÷ 20 × 100 = 110%. The lender's borrowings, not its deposits, funded most of the added loans, so the bank must now either grow deposits faster than loans or keep paying for costlier funding.

body.title: Illustrative credit-deposit ratio before and after the merger

children.text: The consequences followed a predictable chain. The bank had to keep cash reserves and statutory liquidity against deposits and meet priority sector lending norms on a loan book that a housing finance company had never had to hold them against. It had to prioritise deposit growth, which in a competitive market means paying up for deposits. Loan growth had to slow until deposits caught up. Investors focused on deposit growth and margins, and HDFC Bank's share price lagged for much of the year after the merger.

body.text: None of this was hidden. The loan and deposit figures of both companies were public on the day the deal was announced. An investor who had calculated the combined credit-deposit ratio in April 2022 could have anticipated the funding squeeze long before it showed up in quarterly results. The lesson for any merger: combine the two balance sheets yourself on announcement day.

body.title: The metric to watch
body.textWithBlank: After the HDFC merger, investors closely tracked the bank's ___ ratio, which compares its advances with its deposits.
body.explanation: The credit-deposit ratio, or loan-to-deposit ratio, jumped above 100% after the merger because HDFC Ltd brought loans funded mainly by borrowings rather than deposits.

body.title: What happened to HDFC Ltd's subsidiaries?

children.text: HDFC Ltd's major listed and unlisted subsidiaries, including HDFC Life, HDFC ERGO and HDFC Asset Management Company, became subsidiaries of HDFC Bank on the merger. For shareholders of those listed companies, nothing changed in their demat accounts. Only the name of the parent changed.

Some businesses did not fit inside a bank's regulatory perimeter. Before the merger, HDFC Ltd sold a controlling stake in HDFC Credila, its education loan subsidiary. Whenever a non-bank merges into a bank, check which subsidiaries the regulator allows the bank to keep, because forced sales can happen at inconvenient prices.
Step 5: Draw the Lessons

cells: Process
Every approval cleared, and the deal completed in about fifteen months
Over a year of the target trading as a proxy for the acquirer
Share conversion
A clear swap ratio, automatic credit of shares, cash for fractions
Former HDFC Ltd holders now own a bank, with its different risks and earnings drivers
Structure
Holding company layer and cross-holding removed
Subsidiary stakes had to fit bank regulations
Funding
Long-term access to a large deposit franchise
Credit-deposit ratio above 100%, slower loan growth while deposits caught up
Synergies
Structural benefits certain on completion
Funding and cross-selling benefits arrive over years, not quarters

body.title: The double holding
body.scenario: Before the merger, Suresh, a 45-year-old salaried professional, held HDFC Ltd shares worth ₹6 lakh and HDFC Bank shares worth ₹4 lakh, in a ₹25 lakh equity portfolio. He also held two large-cap mutual funds with significant weights in both companies. He did nothing through the merger.
body.prompt: What changed for Suresh, and what should he review?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Concentration: his ₹10 lakh in the two stocks became a single HDFC Bank holding worth roughly the same, 40% of his direct equity portfolio in one bank.
2. Hidden overlap: his large-cap funds also held both companies, and after the merger they held one larger HDFC Bank position, so his total exposure is even higher than 40%.
3. Different business: he now owns a bank with a stretched credit-deposit ratio, not a housing finance company plus a bank. Earnings drivers such as deposit costs and net interest margins now matter more.
4. Tax records: his HDFC Bank shares received in the merger carry forward the cost and holding period of his original HDFC Ltd shares under the conditions covered in Lesson 5.1. He should keep his original purchase records, because his broker's statement may not show the carried-forward cost correctly.
5. Action: decide on a maximum weight for any single stock, count fund exposure too, and rebalance gradually if he is above it, taking capital gains tax into account.

body.title: Apply the HDFC playbook to the next big merger
steps: Classify the deal and identify which company survives
List the stated motives and rank them from most to least certain
Calculate your share entitlement and the post-merger ownership split, allowing for cross-holdings
Combine the two balance sheets yourself and check the key ratios the regulator watches
Identify subsidiaries or businesses that may have to be sold
Review your total exposure, including through mutual funds, once the shares convert

body.label: Screener.in: HDFC Bank
body.description: Look at borrowings, deposits and quarterly profit from FY23 onwards to see the merger's effect on the combined bank's balance sheet.

cards.definition: 42 HDFC Bank shares for every 25 HDFC Ltd shares, or 1.68 per share.
HDFC Ltd's roughly 21% stake in HDFC Bank, cancelled on the merger.
Former HDFC Ltd shareholders owned about 41% of HDFC Bank.
Advances ÷ deposits. It went above 100% after the merger because HDFC Ltd's loans were funded mainly by borrowings.
The RBI's NBFC framework that narrowed the regulatory gap between large NBFCs and banks.

points: The HDFC merger was a parent into subsidiary reverse merger, paid entirely in shares at 42 for every 25, effective 1 July 2023.
Regulation and funding drove it: RBI's scale-based regulation narrowed the gap with banks, and HDFC Bank offered a deposit franchise HDFC Ltd lacked.
Cancelling HDFC Ltd's roughly 21% cross-holding is why its shareholders ended up with about 41% of HDFC Bank.
From announcement day, HDFC Ltd's price tracked 1.68 times HDFC Bank's price, less a spread for time and deal risk.
The big post-merger challenge was funding: the credit-deposit ratio went above 100%, forcing the bank to chase deposits and slow loan growth.
Combine both balance sheets on announcement day and check the ratios regulators care about. That is where the real integration risk shows up.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Share counts and ownership percentages are rounded approximations of publicly disclosed figures. The credit-deposit ratio exercise and chart use simplified illustrative numbers, not the banks' actual balance sheets. Anjali and Suresh are fictional. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
